name: Yara Walsh

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for joining me, Yara. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to AI companies, employers, unions or government, and this conversation is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. What does a normal working day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run the primary crusher and the conveyors at Tallis Ridge, a big open-pit zinc mine. Half my shift I'm in the control room watching screens: feed rates, belt speeds, motor temperatures. The other half I'm out on the plant in a hard hat, checking belts, clearing chutes when they block, and calling the fitters when something sounds wrong.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the control room, honestly. I worked hard to get trained on it, and I like spotting a problem on the screen before it turns into a stoppage. What wears me out is night shift and money. My partner Dan teaches maths at the high school, we just moved into a rental on Ridge Road, and with the bond and my training loan we've got about three weeks of savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a relief for most people, and a bit of a shame for me, because I like the tools. I'd post something like: the useful stuff stays, the hype goes, back to work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be fine. I already use AI to write my shift handover notes, and the crusher at Tallis Ridge still needs someone to hit it with a bar when it jams. The thing that worries me isn't AI, it's that we've got no cushion if the car or the hot water system goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using AI for handovers and fault notes, since it saves me twenty minutes a shift. I'd keep going with my online certificate in process control at night. And Dan and I would try to put a hundred a fortnight aside until we hit two months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty steady. A little impatient, and a little worried about money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How did you start using AI for handover notes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I typed in my rough notes after a messy night, all the alarms and the blocked chute, and asked it to tidy them. My supervisor, Rana, said they were the clearest notes on the crew. Now two others do it too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if the hot water system goes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then it's on the credit card and we eat cheap for a month. Dan's pay is steady but small, and teachers don't get overtime. It's not a disaster, just annoying.

say: I'd say it's a **relief** for most people and a bit of a shame for me.
I'd post that the **useful stuff** stays and the hype goes.
think: My job is **fine** because the crusher still needs a person when it jams.
Our real worry is having **no cushion** for a broken car or hot water.
do: Keep using AI for **handover notes**, saving twenty minutes a shift.
Continue the **process control** certificate at night.
Save **a hundred a fortnight** with Dan until they reach two months.
feel: **Steady**, a little impatient and a little worried about money.
S0.quote: I already use AI to write my shift handover notes, and the crusher at Tallis Ridge still needs someone to hit it with a bar when it jams.
fieldNote: Yara already uses AI daily and taught **two crewmates** to do the same.
Her worry is a **thin cushion** after a bond and a training loan.
Her job mixes **screen work** and hands-on plant checks.

steps.text: Keep running the crusher and conveyors at Tallis Ridge
Use AI to write handover and fault notes each shift
Finish the online process control certificate at night
Save a hundred a fortnight with Dan

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is real and people should get ready instead of arguing about it. I'd tell the crew to learn the new systems, because pretending won't help. I'd keep it balanced, no doom, no cheering.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it hits the part of my job I like most. Process control software with AI built in can watch the feed rate and the belts better than I can, and it doesn't get tired at 3 am. The half of my job that happens on a screen is the half the software wants, and that's the half I was proudest of learning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Rana to put me on the team that sets up the new control software, so I'm the one tuning it, not the one replaced by it. I'd finish the certificate this year instead of next. I'd also start paying off the training loan faster, in case I have to switch roles and take a pay dip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Unsettled, but curious. Like a puzzle I'd rather solve than run from.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would happen to the hands-on half of your job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That probably stays for a while. Someone still has to climb up and clear a chute with a bar. But if the screen half goes, I'd be a plant labourer on a lower grade, and that's a pay cut we can't afford.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who else in the control room would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: George, who's 55 and has done this for thirty years. He reads the plant by sound. He'd be the one they say is too old to retrain, and that would be wrong.

say: I'd say this is **real** and people should get ready, not argue.
I'd tell the crew to **learn the new systems**, with no doom and no cheering.
think: AI **process control** software can watch the plant better than me.
Losing the screen half would leave me a **plant labourer** on lower pay.
do: Ask Rana to join the team **setting up the software**.
Finish the **certificate** this year instead of next.
feel: **Unsettled** but curious, like a puzzle to solve.
S1.quote: The half of my job that happens on a screen is the half the software wants, and that's the half I was proudest of learning.
fieldNote: In Steady Disruption, Yara's **screen work** is hit first, unlike most miners.
She'd rather **tune the software** than be replaced by it.
She worries about **George**, a 55-year-old operator, being written off.

steps.text: Ask to join the team setting up the new control software
Finish the process control certificate this year
Pay extra off the training loan each month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a plan from everyone, companies and government, and we need it this year. I'd say it without picking sides, because both have been slow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it's rough for me. I spent two years learning the control room, and AGI in 2028 would make that the first part of my job to go. The hands-on half lasts till robots arrive around 2031, so I'd have about three years as a plant hand on lower pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start looking for a job that's more hands-on and harder to automate, like an electrical apprenticeship, while I still have the control room pay. I'd use AI to help me study and plan. And Dan and I would cut back hard, no takeaway, one car, to build something before my pay drops.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Shaken. I'm usually the first to adapt, but this is too fast even for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why an electrical apprenticeship, if robots arrive in 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because robots need wiring, and the first generation will break a lot. It's not forever, but it's longer than the screen. And it could take me into renewables if the mine shuts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would Dan's job fare?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Teaching might change but I think kids still need a person in the room. Dan would probably end up carrying us for a few years, which he says is fine. I'd find that hard.

say: I'd say we need **a plan** from companies and government this year.
I'd say it **without picking sides**, because both have been slow.
think: My **control room** skills would be the first part of my job to go.
Robots arrive around **2031**, leaving three years as a plant hand.
do: Look for an **electrical apprenticeship** while still on control room pay.
Use AI to **study** and plan the switch.
Cut back to **one car** and no takeaway.
feel: **Shaken**, because this is too fast even for someone adaptable.
S2.quote: I spent two years learning the control room, and AGI in 2028 would make that the first part of my job to go.
fieldNote: Yara's prized **screen skills** go first, a reversal of the usual miner story.
She'd use the three-year robot gap to move into **electrical work**.
Relying on **Dan's** teacher pay would be hard for her.

steps.text: Apply for an electrical apprenticeship while on control room pay
Use AI tools to study for the electrical trade
Sell the second car and stop takeaway
Rely on Dan's teaching pay during the apprenticeship

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is tight but workable, if people start now. I'd be the one at work saying: pick something and start learning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be okay if I moved fast. Five years is enough for me to stop being the person who watches the crusher and become the person who checks the AI watching the crusher. Even that job goes once AGI arrives in 2031, so I'd use the first three years to get a trade behind me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the process control certificate, then start an electrical apprenticeship by year two. I'd volunteer for every AI trial at Tallis Ridge to stay useful. Dan and I would aim for two months of savings before I take the apprentice pay cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Focused. Nervous about the money, but I know what to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is two months realistic?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I pick up extra night shifts and Dan does summer tutoring, yes. It would be a hard two years. But we'd have a goal, which helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stay at Tallis Ridge?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If they'd take me as an apprentice, yes. If not, I'd look at the solar farm going in north of town. I'd rather not move, Dan's settled at the school.

say: I'd say **five years** is tight but workable if people start now.
I'd tell the crew to **pick something** and start learning.
think: I could become the person who **checks the AI** watching the crusher.
Even that role ends in **2031**, so I'd need a trade too.
do: Start an **electrical apprenticeship** by year two.
Volunteer for every **AI trial** at Tallis Ridge.
Reach **two months** of savings before the apprentice pay cut.
S3.quote: Five years is enough for me to stop being the person who watches the crusher and become the person who checks the AI watching the crusher.
fieldNote: Yara plans a **two-step move**: AI oversight first, then an electrical trade.

steps.text: Start an electrical apprenticeship by year two

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a fair runway, so no one should be caught out. I'd say the companies should help pay for training, and the government should make sure it happens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd feel good about this one. Ten years means I can save, study and switch on my own terms, which is more than my dad ever got when the smelter shut. I'd be 37 in 2036 and 40 when the robots come, with a trade and some savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep running the crusher for a couple of years, finish the certificate and save properly. Then I'd start the electrical apprenticeship, maybe with an eye to solar and batteries. I'd keep using AI every day, at work and for study.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm-ish. Excited, actually, about having a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your dad lost his job when a smelter shut. How does that shape this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A lot. He was 50 and nobody helped him, and he never really worked properly again. I promised myself I'd always have a second thing to fall back on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would still worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Money, in the meantime. Three weeks of savings is still three weeks. If the zinc price drops and Tallis Ridge cuts shifts, that hits before any robot.

I'd say companies should **fund training** and government should make it happen.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. The part of my job I worked hardest for goes first, and I'd have no money to retrain. What would help is paid training, so I'm earning while I learn, and a bit of help with rent during an apprenticeship.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about the cost of adapting. I'm good at learning new things, but being good at learning doesn't pay the rent while you're doing it.

headlineQuote: I'm good at learning new things, but being good at learning doesn't pay the rent while you're doing it.
portrait: Yara, 27, runs the **primary crusher** and conveyors at Tallis Ridge zinc mine.
Her job is half **control room** screens and half hands-on plant checks.
She lives with Dan, a maths teacher, and they have about **three weeks** saved.
She uses AI daily and adapts fast, but faster AGI leaves her **alarmed**.
Her steady plan is an **electrical apprenticeship**, shaped by her dad's smelter job loss.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because her **control room skills** go first with no money to retrain.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid training** so she earns while learning.
